A passenger of the crashed Air Florida Flight 90 is rescued by helicopter from the frozen Potomac River, Virginia. 1982

On January 13, 1982, the Air Florida Boeing 737 crashed into the 14th Street Bridge over the Potomac River just two miles from the White House. It crushed seven occupied vehicles on the bridge and destroyed 97 feet (30 m) of guard rail before it plunged through the ice into the Potomac River. The aircraft was carrying 74 passengers and five crewmembers. Four motorists on the bridge were killed. Four passengers and one flight attendant survived and were rescued from the crash. One of the survivors was rescued by a civilian that dove into the water and swam out to bring her back to shore.

The U.S. Park Police responded with a helicopter flown by Officers Donald W. Usher and Melvin E. Windsor. The pilot hovered low, sometimes with the skids of the helicopter in the water, while Windsor reached the survivors. At times Windsor stood untethered on the helicopter's skid while he dragged people out of the water.

One of the crash survivors, passenger, Arland D. Williams, Jr., handed the rescue line on to others but drowned before he himself could be rescued.

The National Transportation Safety Board determined that the cause of the accident was pilot error. The pilots failed to switch on the engines' internal ice protection systems, used reverse thrust in a snowstorm prior to takeoff, tried to use the jet exhaust of a plane in front of them to melt their own ice, and failed to abort the takeoff even after detecting a power problem while taxiing and visually identifying ice and snow buildup on the wings.
